crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Sepsis Prediction
children.blurb: Sepsis prediction covers models that estimate whether a patient has sepsis or is likely to develop it, usually from electronic health record data such as vital signs, laboratory results, medication orders and nursing notes.

children.name: Acute Kidney Injury Prediction
children.blurb: Acute kidney injury prediction covers models that estimate whether a hospital patient's kidney function is about to decline, usually before creatinine rises far enough to meet the standard diagnostic criteria.

children.name: Ventilator Weaning
children.blurb: Ventilator weaning covers the clinical decision to reduce and then remove mechanical breathing support, and the predictive analytics built around that decision.

children.name: Fall Risk Monitoring
children.blurb: Fall risk monitoring covers systems that estimate how likely a patient is to fall and tools that alert staff when a fall may be happening.

children.name: Staffing and Bed Forecasting
children.blurb: Staffing and bed forecasting covers the models that predict how many nurses, doctors and beds a unit will need over the next shift, day or week.

sections.body: Predictive patient analytics in intensive care is the use of machine learning models on electronic health record data, vital signs, laboratory results and nursing notes to estimate what is likely to happen to a patient in the next few hours or days. In practice these systems run quietly in the background of the intensive care unit, scoring every patient on a schedule and pushing an alert to a clinician when a risk crosses a threshold. Sepsis prediction models watch for the physiological signature of infection plus organ dysfunction and are among the most widely deployed, with several running as part of routine care in large hospital systems. Acute kidney injury models track creatinine, urine output and fluid balance to flag deterioration before it shows up in a single lab value. Ventilator weaning tools estimate readiness for extubation, fall risk monitoring uses bed sensors and mobility data to flag patients likely to fall, and staffing and bed forecasting predicts demand so that units can be resourced ahead of time. This site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and a large share of the ones in active clinical use sit in this category.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The honest picture is mixed. Sepsis models have been validated in many retrospective studies and a few prospective trials, but external validation often shows performance drops when a model moves from the hospital where it was trained to another, and alert fatigue is a real problem when sensitivity is set high. Acute kidney injury prediction is technically strong on the numbers but has struggled to show that acting on the alert changes patient outcomes, which is a different question from whether the model predicts well. Ventilator weaning models are useful as a second opinion but do not replace clinical judgment, and the evidence that they shorten ventilation time is thin. Fall risk monitoring is complicated by false alarms and by the fact that many falls happen in ways sensors do not capture. Staffing and bed forecasting is probably the most mature use, because the target is operational rather than clinical and errors are cheaper. Across all of these, the limits are the same: data quality, shifting clinical practice, and the gap between a good prediction and a good decision. This site also tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, and several of those turn on what a clinician was told and when.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section follow the patient through an intensive care stay and then step back to the unit as a whole. Sepsis Prediction is the entry point for most readers, because sepsis is the condition these systems were first built for and the one with the most public evidence. Acute Kidney Injury Prediction covers a slower, quieter deterioration and shows how the same modeling approach behaves when the signal is spread over days rather than hours. Ventilator Weaning sits at the other end of the stay, where the question is not whether a patient is getting worse but whether they are ready to breathe on their own. Fall Risk Monitoring moves outside the bedside monitor entirely, into sensors and mobility data, and is the clearest example of how a prediction can be right and still not prevent the event. Staffing and Bed Forecasting closes the section by shifting the unit of analysis from one patient to the whole floor, which is where these tools have the least clinical risk and the most operational traction. Read together, the five pages show the same method applied at five different time scales and five different levels of consequence.
